name: Voyager 1
significance: Voyager 1 changed what scientists thought small moons could be. Passing Jupiter in March 1979, it found that Io, a moon about the size of our own, was erupting: at least eight active volcanoes threw sulphur-rich plumes into space, the first active volcanism ever seen beyond Earth. It also found a thin, faint ring around Jupiter, which no one had expected. At Saturn in November 1980 it flew 4,000 km above Titan and found an atmosphere thicker than Earth's, mostly nitrogen, hiding the surface completely, with methane and other hydrocarbons that hinted at chemistry like Earth's before life; it also revealed thousands of ringlets, dark 'spokes' in the rings and small 'shepherd' moons herding the narrow F ring. Choosing the close Titan pass bent its path up out of the plane of the planets, so it visited no more of them. On 1990-02-14, from about 40 AU, it took the last Voyager images: a 'family portrait' of the planets including the 'Pale Blue Dot' view of Earth. In 1998 it became the most distant human-made object, and in 2012 the first to reach interstellar space.
statusNote: Launched 1977-09-05 12:56:01 UT on a Titan IIIE-Centaur from Cape Canaveral (Siddiqi, Beyond Earth; NSSDCA 1977-084A agrees on the date). Horizons' own timeline lists the launch as 1977-Sep-06, but its trajectory section starts on 1977-Sep-5, matching the other sources; 5 September is used. Closest approaches (NSSDC Voyager table, UTC at the spacecraft): Jupiter 1979-03-05 12:05:26 at 4.89 Jupiter radii (about 349,000 km from the centre; 280,000 km above the cloud tops, Siddiqi); Saturn 1980-11-12 23:46:30 at 3.09 Saturn radii (about 186,000 km from the centre; 126,000 km above the cloud tops, Siddiqi). Moon flybys (Siddiqi): Io 21,000 km, Europa 733,760 km, Ganymede 114,710 km, Callisto 126,400 km, Titan 4,000 km (at 05:41 UT on 1980-11-12). Siddiqi dates the Saturn system flyby to 'November 1979' once; it was November 1980. Pale Blue Dot / family portrait: 1990-02-14, about 40 AU from the Sun (Siddiqi). Most distant human-made object from 1998-02-17, at 69.4 AU, passing Pioneer 10 (Siddiqi; NSSDCA). Termination shock 2004-12-16 at 94 AU (Stone et al., Science, 2005; Siddiqi); heliopause into interstellar space 2012-08-25 at about 121.6 AU (Gurnett et al., Science, 2013; Siddiqi). TRAJECTORY: JPL Horizons target -31. Horizons' header describes 1977-09-05 to 1981-01-01 as "a patched conic mission-design type trajectory in which the conics were constructed to approximately match specific events, such as satellite encounters, providing a rough accuracy", and the trajectory after that as a 2022 refit of the 1981-1992 tracking data by R. Jacobson (former Voyager navigation). Horizons is the primary source here, and its Jupiter and Saturn encounters agree with NSSDC's published closest approaches within about 1.3%, so the path is drawn solid. The heliocentric path is Lambert legs between Horizons positions, with planet-centred tours at Jupiter and Saturn, including the Titan flyby (tools/build_voyager.py, tools/build_planet_tour.py). The path stops where Voyager 1 passes 54.514 AU from the Sun, 1.1 times Pluto's farthest distance (its aphelion, 49.558 AU), on 1994-01-06: past that it is out of the Solar System view until a heliosphere layer is added (docs/outer-missions-plan.md section 1). BEYOND THE SOLAR SYSTEM VIEW: the heliosphere layer (zoom out past the Solar System view, or 'Open heliosphere view') draws the path on from the cutoff to 2050, from JPL Horizons (heliospherePath): solid to 2026-11-27, while the craft is still in contact, and dashed after, as a projection. Horizons describes this part of its trajectory as a "Refit of tracking data spanning 1981-1992 (end of two-way coherent transponder data). Done in 2022 by R. Jacobson (former Voyager navigation) using DE440 to generate a new solution and prediction." No two-way tracking has been possible since 1992, so the positions since then are that solution's prediction; they're drawn solid because Horizons is the primary source and the craft is still in contact. On 2026-11-27 it is about 172.5 AU from the Sun.

legs._comment: Heliocentric path built 2026-11-27 by tools/build_voyager.py from JPL Horizons (target -31): Lambert legs between real positions; planet tours spliced in; ends where the craft passes 54.514 AU (1.1 x Pluto's aphelion), the edge of the Solar System view for now.

Jupiter tour built 2026-11-27 by tools/build_planet_tour.py from JPL Horizons (target -31, 1979-03-02 -> 1979-03-09): one planetocentric Lambert arc per piece between real periapses, moon flybys (pinned to the moon's modeled position) and filler waypoints keeping each piece under 60 deg / 1 d.

Saturn tour built 2026-11-27 by tools/build_planet_tour.py from JPL Horizons (target -31, 1980-11-10 -> 1980-11-15): one planetocentric Lambert arc per piece between real periapses, moon flybys (pinned to the moon's modeled position) and filler waypoints keeping each piece under 60 deg / 1 d.
1994-01-06T09:00:00Z: crosses 54.514 AU from the Sun (Horizons, hourly); the Solar System view stops the path here, and the heliosphere layer carries it on.
